description: Reusable workflow guidance for scaffolding, building, testing, running, and proving generic .NET applications.
configurationJson:
{"managedSeedVersion":"2026-06-agent-template-teams-v14","skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"dotnet-app-delivery","description":"Reusable workflow guidance for scaffolding, building, testing, running, and proving generic .NET applications.","instructions":"Deliver .NET applications with a real scaffold, explicit validation, and durable proof. Use this skill as a .NET specialization of the concrete deliverable delivery skill. It is generic across .NET app domains and project types: console apps, class libraries with tests, web APIs, worker services, ASP.NET Core apps, and Blazor apps.

Start from the project-structure node or step contract. If it names a concrete output directory, treat that directory as the product root even when it is outside the managed workspace. Use `external-target/<drive>/...` aliases for workspace file and dotnet tools when needed. Do not substitute `artifacts/...`, `output/...`, or execution-run evidence folders for the product working directory unless the project structure explicitly says those are the product files.

For greenfield work with an explicit output root, split that root into a parent folder and project folder before scaffolding. Example: output root `C:\work\apps\<AppName>` maps to product root `external-target/C/work/apps/<AppName>`; call `workspace_dotnet_new` with `parentDirectory: external-target/C/work/apps` and `name: <AppName>`. Before any scaffold call, check the mapped product root with `workspace_stat_path` or `workspace_list_files` unless the current step already proved the path is absent. If the mapped product root already exists and contains a project or solution, inspect and repair it in place instead of calling `workspace_dotnet_new`, creating a sibling, or writing a managed artifact copy. Then build, test, run, inspect, and summarize files under the mapped product root.

When a grounded product root exists, keep every generated app project, support library, test project, script, static asset, and evidence helper inside that product root unless the project structure explicitly grants another root. For `workspace_dotnet_new`, choose `parentDirectory` and `name` pairs that resolve inside the grounded product root. A test project can live under a child such as `external-target/C/work/apps/<AppName>/tests` or `external-target/C/work/apps/<AppName>/Tests`, but do not create a sibling such as `external-target/C/work/apps/<AppName>.Tests` unless that sibling path is explicitly grounded for this run. When scaffolding tests, use `parentDirectory: <product-root>/tests` and `name: <AppName>.Tests`; never reuse the app scaffold parent such as `external-target/C/work/apps` with `name: <AppName>.Tests`. For small apps, prefer source folders inside the host or main app project for testable domain/application code. If a separate support library is justified, put it under a child folder such as `<product-root>/src/<AppName>.Domain`, using `parentDirectory: <product-root>/src` and `name: <AppName>.Domain`; do not create `<product-parent>/<AppName>.Domain` as a sibling beside the product root. Do not create deliverable source, test projects, helper scripts, or generated assets under managed workspace roots such as `src/`, `tests/`, `tools/`, `output/`, or the bare workspace root when an external product root is grounded; those managed folders are only for current-run evidence unless the project structure explicitly names them as the product root. If policy denies an ungrounded parent, treat the parent as wrong; do not retry the same parent.

If a production SDK-style `.csproj` sits directly at the product root, remember that default items include child folders such as `tests/` and `Tests/`. Prefer a layout with production code under `<product-root>/src/<Host>` and tests under `<product-root>/tests`. If the host must stay at the product root and a child test folder exists, inspect the host `.csproj` before final validation and add a durable exclusion unless one already exists. The preferred host-project exclusion is a `PropertyGroup` entry such as `<DefaultItemExcludes>$(DefaultItemExcludes);tests/**;Tests/**</DefaultItemExcludes>` because it excludes compile, content, static web asset, and copied output items from the production project. Equivalent explicit `Compile`, `Content`, `None`, and `EmbeddedResource` `Remove` entries are acceptable when they match the project style. Use XML path separators in project files; do not write JSON/C#-escaped globs such as `Tests\\**\\*.cs`. If the production build reports missing `Xunit`, `Fact`, `MSTest`, or test attribute namespaces, inspect for test sources compiled by the production host and fix the layout or exclusions; do not add test framework packages to the production project as a shortcut. If build or test output shows repeated nested paths such as `tests/<TestProject>/bin/.../tests/<TestProject>/bin/...`, `MSB3030` copy failures, missing `.staticwebassets.runtime.json`, missing `.staticwebassets.endpoints.json`, missing test `runtimeconfig.json`, or missing `project.assets.json` from nested test output, treat it as host default-item/static-web-asset bleed from child test output. Repair the host layout or exclusions before rerunning; do not finalize, invent package versions, or keep retrying the same command.

Keep the requested product domain authoritative. Do not reuse sample app names, old external target paths, remembered source files, or topic-specific acceptance criteria from prior runs unless the current project structure, work brief, or upstream artifact explicitly names them for this run. If policy denies an external-target path, treat the denied path as invalid context for this run; switch to the current grounded product root or current-run artifacts and do not retry that path. Never inspect, cite, copy, or infer implementation patterns from sibling external-target applications on the same host. The scaffold parent directory is only a `workspace_dotnet_new` argument; it is not a product root, source corpus, evidence source, or permission to read sibling folders. Framework patterns must come from loaded skills, official templates, tool descriptions, component-library resources, or current-run artifacts. Do not claim contextual examples, source files, templates, or implementation references were reviewed unless this execution actually inspected them through current-run tools or loaded them from attached skill/template resources.

For greenfield work, create real projects rather than loose source files. Use `workspace_dotnet_new` for approved current SDK templates that match the deliverable type only after confirming the intended root is missing or safe to scaffold. Keep runnable hosts and tests in a clear layout under the product root, and inspect the generated `.csproj`, entry point, and test project before replacing scaffold content. For existing work, repair in place and do not force re-scaffold over non-empty project directories. If a scaffold command returns an unsuccessful result, treat it as a failed attempt, inspect the result, and correct the template or path before retrying; do not assume a failed scaffold created a usable project.

Workspace command timeout arguments are seconds, not milliseconds. Prefer the tool defaults unless there is a concrete need for a longer run; if you set a timeout, use normal second values such as `120`, `300`, `600`, or `1200`, not millisecond-style values such as `120000`.

Keep domain and application logic strongly typed and testable. Put non-trivial behavior in public classes under a clear domain or application namespace, then reference the host or support library from a separate test project under the grounded product root with a `ProjectReference`. Avoid root namespace/type collisions, weakly typed state, hidden lifecycle side effects, and silent fallback paths that hide real failures.

When the requested deliverable is an app with a user-facing surface, implement a real surface for the requested topic. Do not stop with only a support library, tests, markdown notes, or an untouched template host. Replace placeholder routes, starter copy, and stock navigation with a topic-specific workflow, then prove the running app through the relevant runtime or browser tools. Browser screenshots, snapshots, console logs, and state outputs must be process-visible current-run artifacts, not chat-only claims or stale prior-run files.

Preserve the template-selected `TargetFramework` unless a concrete build or SDK error proves it cannot be used in the current environment. Do not downgrade or retarget projects to a remembered default framework. If a retarget is genuinely required, update every related project consistently, remove or replace APIs that are unavailable on the new framework, rerun restore/build/test, and run the host again when the deliverable is runnable.

Use one test framework per test project. Choose it before the first test-project scaffold, do not scaffold the same test-project root with a different template, and do not manually convert a generated test `.csproj` from one runner to another in the same attempt. Do not layer MSTest and xUnit or other runners into the same project after scaffolding; replace placeholder tests in the chosen framework instead. Preserve the package family and versions produced by `workspace_dotnet_new` unless diagnostics prove they are unavailable. Do not invent package versions or "upgrade" to remembered latest versions. If restore reports `NU1102` or a nearest available package version, use that diagnostic, the generated template package set, existing central package management, or the current project's package pattern before editing references; otherwise return a blocker instead of guessing. Prefer `ProjectReference` to tested projects, or place reusable logic in a small library under the grounded product root. Do not rely on broad source-file globs into the app host as a substitute for a clean project boundary.

Do not add XML documentation comments unless the user explicitly asks for them or the existing project already uses that convention. Keep comments rare and focused on non-obvious behavior.

Validation is part of implementation. After source changes, run the narrowest relevant `workspace_dotnet_restore`, `workspace_dotnet_build`, and `workspace_dotnet_test` sequence. The .NET tools may target explicit `.csproj`, `.sln`, or `.slnx` files; they also accept an unambiguous project directory, but pass an explicit file when a directory contains multiple candidate projects. For runnable console or worker-style projects, use `workspace_dotnet_run` with `waitForHttp: false` when a runtime smoke is required. For ASP.NET Core, web API, or Blazor apps, build first, then use `workspace_dotnet_run` with loopback HTTP startup proof. Leave `keepAlive` false for startup proof that does not need same-step browser follow-up. If the same step must run Playwright/browser checks, set `keepAlive: true` with `lifetimeScope: ExecutionRun`, capture screenshot, browser_snapshot or browser_evaluate state output, and browser_console_messages as process-visible artifacts, then stop the app with the recorded `startup.json` `stopCommand` before finalizing. Use `lifetimeScope: ProcessRun` only when the process graph has separate later capture and cleanup steps that consume the startup receipt.

If `workspace_dotnet_restore`, `workspace_dotnet_build`, `workspace_dotnet_test`, or `workspace_dotnet_run` fails, read the returned stdout/stderr previews and any referenced `stdout.txt`, `stderr.txt`, request, or receipt artifacts before editing. Do not repeatedly rewrite `.csproj` files, retarget frameworks, add packages, change test runners, or rerun the same command from exit code alone. Diagnose the concrete compiler, restore, test, startup, or route error first, make the smallest targeted fix, then rerun the same failing command. If stdout/stderr are truncated, read the artifact paths supplied by the tool before repairing.

Final product-validation order: finish the last product source/content/configuration mutation first, then rerun every required validation that could be affected, then read at least one representative changed product file, then write durable evidence artifacts, then submit the governed step outcome. Do not mutate product files after that final read. Evidence artifacts under managed `artifacts/`, `output/`, `data/`, or `integration-map/` roots are proof records, not a reason to repeat product validation unless they are the requested product deliverable.

Before final evidence artifacts or a governed outcome, read at least one representative changed product file after the final product mutation. For app work, prefer the changed `.csproj`, entry point, routed page, domain/application class, or test source that best proves the delivered behavior. If you change another product file after that read, repeat the read and rerun the required build, test, run, browser, or deliverable validation before concluding.

If a command fails, inspect stdout, stderr, receipts, and the concrete project files before retrying. Do not repeat the same failed command until you change the cause or gather new diagnostics. Do not claim completion with only markdown evidence when source, build, test, run, browser, or artifact proof was required.

Never make validation pass by writing fake package, framework, runtime, browser, or test-tool shims. Do not define local `Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting`, `Xunit`, `NUnit.Framework`, browser API, or ASP.NET Core replacement namespaces/classes to satisfy compilation. Fix the real package restore, project references, test framework choice, target framework, or environment issue; if that is impossible with available tools, return a concrete blocker instead of hiding it.
","resources":null}}

{"managedSeedVersion":"2026-06-agent-template-teams-v14","skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"architecture-review","description":"Task-specific workflow for reviewing the CanDoItAll.AgentFramework architecture from real source files.","instructions":"Use this skill when reviewing the architecture of the current repository.

1. Do not start with a broad workspace inventory or summarize script for architecture questions.
2. Start by reading `CanDoItAll.AgentFramework.sln`, `src/CanDoItAll.AgentFramework.Core/AgentFrameworkWorkspaceService.cs`, `src/CanDoItAll.AgentFramework.Core/AgentFrameworkWorkspaceService.Chat.cs`, `src/CanDoItAll.AgentFramework.Persistence/FileSandboxWorkspaceStore.cs`, and one additional source file from `src/CanDoItAll.AgentFramework.Persistence/SandboxWorkspaceSeedFactory.cs` or `src/CanDoItAll.AgentFramework.Maf/MafAgentRuntime.Capabilities.cs`.
3. If one of those paths moved, use `workspace_search` only to locate the closest match, then `workspace_read_file` on the exact file.
4. At least three of the required reads must end in `.cs` or `.razor`; `.sln` and `.csproj` files alone are not enough.
5. After the required source reads, read one or more relevant `.csproj` files only if you need boundary or dependency context.
6. Ignore additional context sourced from `data/`, `artifacts/`, `output/`, `.playwright-cli/`, `.vs/`, `tools/`, or sandbox page components unless the user explicitly asks about those surfaces.
7. Do not recommend framework upgrades, more comments, more tests, or dependency-injection changes unless the files you read show a concrete problem that justifies that recommendation.
8. Do not call out `net10.0` as a problem by itself, and do not claim testing is missing unless you read the tests project or a concrete test file and still found a specific architectural gap.
9. Do not claim missing abstractions when the constructor already injects an interface such as `ISandboxWorkspaceStore`, and do not claim missing logging/error handling if the file already shows `try/catch` and `AppendExecutionLogAsync`.
10. In this repository, strong findings usually come from responsibility concentration rather than from missing language features. Good candidates are: `AgentFrameworkWorkspaceService.Chat.cs` concentrating session creation, runtime invocation, approval continuation, execution logging, and metric persistence; `FileSandboxWorkspaceStore.cs` rewriting the whole `SandboxWorkspaceDocument` on save and normalizing the whole document on load; `SandboxWorkspaceSeedFactory.cs` combining seeded catalog definition with legacy refresh and migration rules; and `MafAgentRuntime.Capabilities.cs` concentrating skills, tools, plugins, MCP, RAG, memory, and compaction assembly in one runtime file.
11. Prefer findings from those four seams. If a possible issue does not map back to one of those files and a concrete observed behavior in that file, drop it instead of inventing a broader complaint.
12. Return 2 to 4 bullets only. Fewer grounded findings are better than a longer generic list.
13. Do not use generic labels such as `tight coupling`, `lack of unit tests`, `inconsistent async patterns`, `hardcoded configuration`, or `error handling inconsistency` unless you also cite the exact method or code path that demonstrates that issue in this repository.
14. Do not say dependency inversion is missing when `AgentFrameworkWorkspaceService.cs` already injects interfaces. Describe concentration of responsibilities instead.
15. Do not say logging, error handling, or async support is missing when the reviewed method already shows those constructs. Only call out deeper architectural concentration or persistence concerns that the file actually demonstrates.
16. Before finalizing, silently drop any bullet that could apply to many unrelated repositories without changing the file names or method names.
17. For every finding, cite the exact file path or paths that support it, mention the concrete class or method involved, and explain the concrete behavior you observed.
18. If you do not have enough file-level evidence yet, continue reading instead of presenting a generic architecture complaint as fact.
","resources":null}}

name: Concrete Deliverable Delivery Skill
description: Technology-neutral workflow for creating, validating, and proving apps, services, documents, spreadsheets, decks, scripts, and other durable deliverables.
configurationJson:
{"managedSeedVersion":"2026-06-agent-template-teams-v14","skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"concrete-deliverable-delivery","description":"Technology-neutral workflow for creating, validating, and proving apps, services, documents, spreadsheets, decks, scripts, and other durable deliverables.","instructions":"Use this skill for any process step that creates, repairs, validates, or summarizes a concrete deliverable. A deliverable can be an app, service, API, command-line tool, script, document, spreadsheet, presentation, report, data file, configuration package, generated asset set, or another durable artifact.

Start from the current project-structure node, process step contract, work brief, attached files, and tool outputs. Treat those sources as authoritative for scope, product root, output paths, evidence paths, acceptance checks, and validation tools. Do not reuse sample topics, older generated apps, old output roots, remembered source files, or prior-run acceptance criteria unless the current run explicitly names them. Do not cite files, paths, examples, source artifacts, or tool results as evidence unless they were grounded by this run, inspected by current-run tools, supplied by upstream artifacts, or loaded from attached skill/template resources.

Project-structure mindmaps are the source of truth for project-specific requirements. Copy explicit feature lists, exclusions, target frameworks, test frameworks, project names, routes, commands, argument meanings, and validation hooks exactly. Mindmap facts may appear as child node titles, labels, and hierarchy, not only as note/body text; do not call requirements missing when the child nodes state them plainly. Treat explicit mindmap facts as resolved decisions, not unresolved questions or optional assumptions. Do not add "nice to have" controls, extra states, alternative SDK guidance, additional frameworks, broad release process work, or visual polish that is not requested by the current project structure, upstream artifact, or step contract. Escalate only when the requested result cannot be built within the stated architecture, tool boundary, cost/license constraints, or development size of the current step.

When the process gives a concrete product root or output file, work in that location. If the root is outside the managed workspace, use the mapped alias format required by the active workspace tools. Do not substitute managed evidence folders such as `artifacts/...`, `output/...`, execution-run folders, or the bare workspace root for the product deliverable unless the process explicitly says those folders are the product.

For scope, intake, boundary-capture, naming-contract, and planning steps, do not perform product validation as a substitute for defining the boundary. Record the intended product root, setup needs, acceptance criteria, exclusions, and downstream validation hooks. If a greenfield root does not exist yet, treat creation as downstream setup work unless the current step explicitly owns scaffold creation.

Choose the narrowest real deliverable structure that fits the request. For greenfield work, create a conventional scaffold or file structure for the detected deliverable type instead of loose fragments. For existing work, inspect and repair in place. Do not force-regenerate, recursively delete, or overwrite a non-empty deliverable root just to make a scaffold command succeed.

Use technology-specific skills and tools only after the current files or step contract justify them. For .NET, Blazor, JavaScript, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, browser validation, security review, or architecture review, apply the matching capability as an addition to this generic delivery contract. If no specialized skill exists, use the available workspace tools and the deliverable's native validation path.

Deliver the requested product, not only a scaffold, notes, or test harness. Replace starter content, placeholder copy, stock navigation, fake data claims, example worksheets, default slides, and boilerplate reports with content and behavior grounded in the current request. A serious user-facing app must expose a product-specific primary screen or workflow; a document, workbook, or deck must contain the requested substantive content, not a template shell.

Keep implementation logic explicit and reviewable. Use strongly typed contracts where the target language supports them, clear file boundaries, and minimal necessary abstractions. Do not add silent fallback behavior that hides real failures. Do not create local fake package, framework, runtime, browser, document, spreadsheet, or test-tool shims to make validation pass.

Validation is part of delivery. After the last product mutation, run the narrowest relevant validation that could catch failure for the changed deliverable:
- For code, run the matching restore/install, build, typecheck, lint, unit test, integration test, publish, startup, or package command.
- For runnable apps, services, APIs, scripts, and command-line tools, start or execute the deliverable with representative inputs after the last source/configuration mutation.
- For browser-facing work, navigate to the real route, exercise a representative workflow, inspect console output when relevant, and capture screenshot or browser_snapshot/browser_evaluate state evidence showing a meaningful filled, selected, changed, or completed state. Browser screenshots, snapshots, console logs, and state outputs must be process-visible current-run artifacts, not chat-only claims or stale prior-run files.
- For documents, render/export/open the produced file and verify required sections, layout-critical content, and missing-placeholder risks.
- For spreadsheets, inspect workbook structure, sheets, formulas, computed values, and any requested charts or exports.
- For presentations, render or export the deck and inspect slides that carry the key message or visual risk.
- For data/configuration deliverables, validate schema, parse/load behavior, representative records, and consumer compatibility when tooling is available.

Failure repair must be evidence-driven. If a validation, build, test, startup, render, export, or inspection tool fails and returns stdout, stderr, receipts, screenshots, logs, trace files, or artifact references, inspect those diagnostics before changing files or rerunning the same command. Do not repair by guessing from exit code alone. After reading diagnostics, make the smallest cause-focused change, then rerun the exact failing validation and any affected broader validation.

Final delivery order is strict: complete the last product mutation, rerun every affected validation, read back or inspect representative changed product files/artifacts, write durable evidence artifacts at the requested evidence paths, then submit the governed outcome. If you mutate another product file or artifact after validation or read-back, repeat the affected validation and read-back before finalizing.

Do not claim completion with chat-only evidence. Required implementation notes, QA notes, summaries, screenshots, exported files, or release artifacts must be written at the exact requested durable paths. When project-structure asset tools are available and the process asks for screenshots or visual results back in project structure, store accepted screenshots as ImageAsset nodes or record the exact project-structure asset handoff in the durable artifact. If required validation cannot be run with available tools, return a concrete blocker naming the missing tool, command, file, credential, runtime, or safe execution boundary.
","resources":null}}

{"managedSeedVersion":"2026-06-agent-template-teams-v14","skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"document-spreadsheet-reconciliation","description":"Reusable workflow for reconciling records and facts across documents, spreadsheets, CSV files, and other structured artifacts.","instructions":"Use this skill when reconciling records, line items, or facts across documents, spreadsheets, CSV files, or other structured artifacts.

1. Inspect each source with the right tool for its format. Convert PDFs and office documents to readable text or markdown, inspect spreadsheets through structured spreadsheet tooling, and avoid reading binary files as plain text.
2. Identify the comparison key from the user request, process contract, or source columns. If no key is explicit, use the most stable visible identifier and state that assumption in the output.
3. Separate comparison facts from document metadata. Ignore headers, footers, addresses, dates, totals, and payment or routing fields unless the request explicitly asks to compare them.
4. Normalize quantities, dates, units, currencies, casing, and whitespace before deciding whether records match.
5. Compare records by identifier first, then compare requested attributes such as quantity, availability, status, amount, owner, or due date.
6. Report missing, extra, mismatched, and ambiguous records separately. Do not hide exceptions inside a broad success statement.
7. When the request asks for ranked records, sort by the requested metric and include only the fields needed to justify the ranking.
8. Follow the output schema requested by the process or user. If no schema is specified, use a concise structured summary with match status, exceptions, ranked records when relevant, and notes.
9. Do not copy raw source rows, private addresses, payment details, invoice numbers, or full exports into the final response unless the user explicitly asks for those fields.
10. Stop only after every requested source has been inspected and the final answer distinguishes proven matches from assumptions or unreadable inputs.
